summary: Describes the canonical form of an XML document, a standard way of writing it so allowed differences such as spacing do not matter. This helps when comparing or signing XML. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Two XML files can hold exactly the same information and still differ in how they are written down. Canonical XML defines one agreed way to write an XML document down, so that two files can be compared byte for byte. That matters most for digital signatures, which must not break when a file is merely reformatted.

questions: how are attributes sorted in canonical xml
subtitle: One agreed way to write an XML document down, so that two copies can be compared byte for byte

tldr.problem: XML 1.0 and Namespaces allow the same information to be written down in several different ways, so two documents that mean the same thing can differ in their entity structure, their attribute order and their character encoding.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines a canonical form: a physical representation of a document produced by a fixed method. The document is parsed into the XPath data model, the nodes are walked in a defined order, and each node type has a fixed way of being written out, ending in UTF-8.
tldr.outcome: Two documents with the same canonical form are logically equivalent within the application context, which is what lets a digital signature survive a harmless reformatting. The memo also lists three kinds of information the canonical form loses, all of which the application has to handle.

facts.label: Input the method accepts
facts.value: An XPath node-set or an octet stream of well-formed XML

facts.label: Node types in the XPath data model
facts.value: 7: root, element, comment, processing instruction, text, attribute, namespace

facts.label: Information lost by canonicalization
facts.value: Base URI, notations and unparsed entities, attribute types

facts.label: Output encoding
facts.value: UTF-8 without a leading byte order mark

today: RFC 3076 is an Informational memo that has not been obsoleted or updated. It specifies an algorithm rather than a protocol, and it is written to be re-run: canonicalizing an already canonical document changes nothing, as long as that document is well-formed XML.

sections.title: Why Canonical XML Exists
sections.content:
XML 1.0 defines the syntax of XML documents, and Namespaces in XML adds syntax and semantics for namespaces. It is possible for XML documents that are equivalent for the purposes of many applications to differ in physical representation: they may differ in their entity structure, in attribute ordering, and in character encoding. The goal of this specification is to establish a method for determining whether two documents are identical, or whether an application has not changed a document, except for the transformations permitted by XML 1.0 and Namespaces.

The method produces a canonical form. Except for limitations regarding a few unusual cases, if two documents have the same canonical form then the two documents are logically equivalent within the given application context. The converse does not hold: two documents may have differing canonical forms and still be equivalent in a given context, because application-specific equivalence rules, which no generalized XML specification could account for, may apply.

The application the memo has in mind is testing whether the information content of a document has changed. Because XML applications tend to take liberties with changes that do not affect the information content, this is done by comparing the canonical form of the original document before processing with the canonical form of the result. For a digital signature over the canonical form, the digest calculation is then oblivious to changes in the physical representation, provided the changes are logically equivalent under XML 1.0 or Namespaces. During signature generation the digest is computed over the canonical form; the document is then transferred to the relying party, which validates the signature by reading the document and computing the digest of the canonical form of the received document. The equivalence of the two digests, and hence of the canonical forms over which they were computed, is what shows that the information content has not been altered since it was signed.
sections.plainLanguage: XML lets the same information be written down in several ways: attributes in a different order, an entity instead of the text it stands for, a different character encoding. Canonical XML picks one way of writing each document down, so two files can be compared byte for byte. That is what lets a digital signature survive a harmless reformatting.

sections.title: The Data Model and Document Order
sections.content:
The input to the method is either an XPath node-set or an octet stream holding a well-formed XML document, and the second input is a flag saying whether comments should be kept. If the input is an octet stream, an XML processor converts it into the XPath data model by performing four tasks in order: normalize line feeds, normalize attribute values, replace CDATA sections with their character content, and resolve character and parsed entity references. The input must be well-formed but need not be valid, though the attribute value normalization and entity reference resolution must behave as in a validating processor. Nodes for default attributes, declared in the attribute list but not specified, are created in each element, so the document type declaration is used to help build the canonical form even though it is not kept in it.

Several details of the data model matter. The document is represented in UCS characters, and implementations must use processors that support UTF-8 and UTF-16 and translate into the UCS character domain, where the leading byte order mark of UTF-16 is treated as an artifact of encoding and stripped. All whitespace inside the root document element must be preserved, including whitespace in external entities, while whitespace outside the root document element must be discarded. In the data model there are seven node types, root, element, comment, processing instruction, text, attribute and namespace, and a single root node whose children are the processing instructions and comments outside the document element together with the top-level element itself.

Because a node-set is unordered, the method imposes its own document order on the namespace and attribute nodes of each element: they sit after the element but before any of its children; namespace nodes come before attribute nodes; namespace nodes are sorted lexicographically by local name, with the default namespace node, which has no local name, lexicographically least; and attribute nodes are sorted with namespace URI as the primary key and local name as the secondary key, an empty namespace URI being lexicographically least. Lexicographic comparison is based on UCS codepoint values, which is equivalent to lexicographic ordering based on UTF-8.
sections.plainLanguage: The document is first turned into a tree of nodes using the model from XPath: elements, text, attributes, namespaces, comments and instructions, gathered under one root. The method then walks that tree in a fixed order, so the result does not depend on how the file happened to be written. Attributes are sorted by the namespace they belong to and then by name, and namespace declarations always come before attributes.

sections.title: How Each Node Is Written Out
sections.content:
The node-set is turned into the canonical form by generating the representative characters for each node in the node-set in ascending document order and encoding the result in UTF-8 without a leading byte order mark. No node is processed twice. The result for a node depends on its type and on whether it is in the node-set: a node outside the set generates no text of its own, but its namespace and attribute axes and its children are still processed, because an omitted node can still affect its descendants, for instance by adding to their namespace context.

The rules for each node type are short. The root node contributes the results of its children that are in the node-set, and generates no byte order mark, XML declaration or anything from the document type declaration. An element in the node-set produces an open angle bracket, its QName, the namespace axis, the attribute axis, a close angle bracket, its children, then an open angle bracket, a forward slash and its QName again. An element outside the node-set contributes only its namespace and attribute axes and its children. On the namespace axis, an empty default namespace is generated only when the element owns the axis and its nearest ancestor in the node-set has a non-empty default namespace, which removes unnecessary occurrences; the namespace node for the prefix xml is omitted when its value is the XML namespace URI. A namespace node is ignored when the nearest ancestor element in the node-set already has a namespace node with the same local name and value.

An attribute is written as a space, its QName, an equals sign, a double quotation mark, the modified string value and a closing double quotation mark. The string value is modified by replacing ampersands, open angle brackets and double quotation marks with character references, and the whitespace characters #x9, #xA and #xD with character references written in uppercase hexadecimal without leading zeroes. Text nodes are written as their string value with ampersands, open angle brackets, closing angle brackets and #xD replaced by character references. A processing instruction is written as the opening symbol, the target name, a space and the string value if it is not empty, then the closing symbol. A comment is omitted entirely from canonical XML without comments, and written as the opening symbol, the string value and the closing symbol in canonical XML with comments. The QName of a node uses the namespace prefix that appeared in the input document.
sections.plainLanguage: Every node has a fixed way of being written. Elements become a start tag and an end tag, never the short empty form. Attribute values are always in double quotes, and the characters that could break the markup are written as character references instead. Comments are either kept or dropped depending on the flag. The whole result is written as UTF-8 with no byte order mark.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The memo works through seven examples. The first takes a document with an XML declaration, a stylesheet processing instruction, a document type declaration, a comment inside the document element and two comments outside it. The canonical form without comments loses the XML declaration, loses the document type declaration, normalises the whitespace outside the document element so that the first character is an angle bracket and single line breaks separate the processing instructions and comments, and drops the comments along with the delimiters outside the document element. The form with comments keeps the comment inside the document element and the two outside it.

The second example shows that whitespace is retained everywhere inside the document element, whether between consecutive start tags, between consecutive end tags, between an end tag and a start tag, or inside character content. The third example covers start and end tags: empty elements become start-end tag pairs, whitespace inside start and end tags is normalised, namespace declarations come before attributes, both are sorted lexicographically, namespace prefixes from the original document are kept, superfluous namespace declarations are eliminated, and a default attribute is added. The example also notes why one attribute sorts before another: the primary key is the namespace URI rather than the prefix, and the default namespace is not applied to unqualified attributes, so an unqualified attribute has an empty namespace URI.

The fourth example covers character modifications and character references: a character reference for a carriage return followed by a line feed becomes a carriage return reference and a line feed, a numeric character reference is replaced by the character itself, CDATA sections are replaced by their content, attribute value delimiters become double quotes, and attribute values are normalised. The fifth covers entity references: an internal parsed entity and an external parsed entity are replaced by their content, including the whitespace around them, while an external unparsed entity is left as an attribute value. The sixth shows transcoding, with a document written in ISO-8859-1 and a copyright character coming out as the two UTF-8 octets C2 and A9. The seventh shows a document subset, where an element is picked out with a predicate expression and the canonical form carries the namespace declaration of an omitted parent so that the meaning of the element is preserved.
sections.plainLanguage: Seven worked examples show the rules in action. A file with comments and processing instructions outside its main element comes out with the XML declaration and document type declaration removed. A file with odd spacing keeps the spacing inside its elements but tidies the tags themselves. A file with attributes in a strange order comes out with them sorted, empty elements written in full, and any duplicate namespace declaration dropped.

sections.title: Why the Rules Are What They Are
sections.content:
The final section explains the decisions. The XML declaration is omitted because the encoding is always UTF-8 and the absence of a version number unambiguously indicates XML 1.0, though future versions of XML will require a declaration, so this method may need modification for them.

Character model normalization is left out of scope. The Unicode standard allows several representations of a precomposed character, so two documents that are equivalent for most applications may contain differing character sequences, and a normalized form was being prepared by the W3C. But many XML 1.0 processors do not perform that normalization, and applications that must solve the problem typically enforce it whenever content is created, so it was moved out of scope. The processor preparing the input is still required to use Normalization Form C when converting from an encoding that is not UCS-based.

The other decisions follow from the same kind of reasoning. Whitespace outside the document element is handled so that processing instructions and comments there are separated from markup by a line feed, even when the root node or the document element is omitted from the output. Namespace prefixes are not rewritten: an earlier draft did rewrite them so that documents with equivalent declarations would be identical, but prefixes can now carry information, since an XPath expression in an attribute value or element content can refer to one, and rewriting them would change the meaning of the document. The XPath data model puts all namespace nodes before all attribute nodes, which replaces the earlier draft's alternation between them. Superfluous namespace declarations are dropped, whether for an empty default namespace, a non-empty default namespace or a prefix binding, when the immediate parent element in the canonical form already has an equivalent declaration in scope; the root document element is handled specially, since it has no parent, and all of its declarations are kept except an empty default namespace. This costs no more than a constant factor in processing time and memory, and it removes stray xmlns declarations from applications that barely use namespaces. In document subsets, an empty default namespace in an omitted ancestor is propagated so that a descendant does not silently pick up the ancestor's namespace. Finally, attributes are sorted with the namespace URI as the primary key and the local name as the secondary key, because that is closer to the intent of the XML Namespaces specification, which identifies namespaces by URI and local name rather than by prefix and local name; the effect is that all attributes in one namespace group together.
sections.plainLanguage: Each rule has a reason. The declaration is dropped because the output is always UTF-8 XML 1.0. Prefixes are left alone because a prefix can carry meaning, for example when an XPath expression refers to one. Duplicate namespace declarations are removed because the parent usually already says the same thing. And attributes are sorted by the namespace they live in rather than by their prefix, which is how the namespaces specification itself identifies them.

sections.title: Limitations and Security
sections.content:
The memo is candid about what canonicalization loses. The security issues are discussed here and nowhere else, and they come from information that the data model does not carry. Three things are lost: the base URI, especially in content derived from the replacement text of external general parsed entity references; notations and external unparsed entity references; and attribute types in the document type declaration.

A document containing a relative URI is only operational when accessed from a specific URI that provides the proper base URI, and if the document contains external general parsed entity references to content with relative URIs, those relative URIs will not be operational in the canonical form, because the canonical form replaces the entity reference with internal content and so implicitly changes the default base URI. The usual fix is to add support for the xml:base attribute and add appropriate attributes to the document element and to all top-level elements in external entities; applications also often have the chance to resolve relative URIs before a canonical form is needed, for example during signature generation, and the processing should then create a new document with absolute URIs.

Losing external unparsed entity references and the notations that bind them means canonical forms cannot properly distinguish documents that incorporate unparsed data that way, which is unusual because most XML processors discard the document type declaration anyway, and where a document must go through more than one processor the XML design indicates unparsed data with a URI in the attribute value. Losing attribute types has different effects depending on the type: attributes of type ID cease to be ID attributes, so XPath expressions that refer to the canonical form using the id() function cease to operate, and attributes of enumerated type and of type ID, IDREF, IDREFS, NMTOKEN, NMTOKENS and NOTATION are no longer appropriately constrained if the canonical form replaces the original document. An application can avoid this by prepending an appropriate document type declaration before using the canonical form further. The limitations are not severe, and the memo notes it would be possible to resolve them in a future version of XML canonicalization if, for example, a new version of XPath were created based on the XML Information Set.
sections.plainLanguage: Canonicalization drops a few things that XML can carry, and each drop can matter. Relative addresses lose the base address they were written against, so they may point somewhere else in the canonical copy. Files referenced by a document type declaration lose their link. And attributes lose their declared type, so an identifier attribute stops being an identifier and code that looks it up by name stops working. Each of these can be handled by the application, but only if the application knows to do it.

viz.caption: THE CANONICAL FORM OF THE START AND END TAG EXAMPLE

data.title: Canonical form
data.code:
<doc>
   <e1></e1>
   <e2></e2>
   <e3 id="elem3" name="elem3"></e3>
   <e4 id="elem4" name="elem4"></e4>
   <e5 xmlns="http://example.org" xmlns:a="http://www.w3.org"
xmlns:b="http://www.ietf.org" attr="I'm" attr2="all"
b:attr="sorted" a:attr="out"></e5>
   <e6 xmlns:a="http://www.w3.org">
      <e7 xmlns="http://www.ietf.org">
         <e8 xmlns="">
            <e9 xmlns:a="http://www.ietf.org" attr="default"></e9>
         </e8>
      </e7>
   </e6>
</doc>

items.title: No XML declaration
items.text: The output is always UTF-8, and no version number means XML 1.0.

items.title: No character model normalization
items.text: Applications that need it enforce it when content is created, so it was left out of scope.

items.title: No prefix rewriting
items.text: A prefix can carry meaning, as when an XPath expression refers to one.

items.title: Namespaces before attributes
items.text: The XPath data model puts all namespace nodes before all attribute nodes.

items.title: Superfluous declarations dropped
items.text: A declaration is omitted when the parent already has an equivalent one in scope.

items.title: Attributes sorted by namespace URI
items.text: Namespace URI is the primary key and local name the secondary key, so one namespace groups together.
